description: Pre-screening readiness, common injuries, RICE recovery, and performance-enhancing drugs in sport.
content_html:
Preventing Injury Before It Happens

Injury is one of the biggest barriers to consistent training and performance. Preventing injury requires a proactive approach: screening individuals before they train, applying the principles of training correctly to avoid overuse, using appropriate equipment, and following the rules of the activity. When injury does occur, the correct immediate treatment limits damage and speeds recovery.

The PARQ: Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire

Before starting a new training programme, an individual should complete a PARQ (Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire). The PARQ is a short set of questions asking about cardiovascular health, recent illness, known medical conditions, bone or joint problems, pregnancy, prescription medication and any other reasons that might make vigorous exercise unsuitable without medical guidance. If a person answers “yes” to any question, they are advised to consult a doctor before beginning training. The PARQ protects both the individual and the coach — it ensures that exercise is safe and that any training programme is adapted to the person’s health status.

Injury Prevention Strategies

Applying the principles of training correctly is the first line of defence against overuse injuries. Increasing training load too quickly — violating progressive overload — is the single most common cause of overuse injury in sport. Shin splints, stress fractures and tendinopathy all develop when training volume or intensity increases faster than the body can adapt. A structured programme with planned rest and recovery prevents this.

Additional prevention strategies include: following the rules of the activity to minimise contact injuries; using appropriate protective clothing and equipment (helmets, shin pads, gum shields, braces); and checking facilities and equipment before use to remove hazards such as uneven surfaces, damaged apparatus or unsuitable footwear.

Common Injuries in Sport

Several injury types appear on the specification. Concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head. Symptoms include headache, confusion, dizziness and nausea. Any athlete suspected of concussion must be removed from play immediately and not return until medically cleared — the “if in doubt, sit them out” protocol. Fractures are breaks in bone. A dislocation occurs when joint surfaces are forced out of alignment, commonly at the shoulder or finger. A sprain is damage to a ligament at a joint; a strain is damage to a muscle or tendon. Torn cartilage, most commonly the meniscus of the knee, occurs when the fibrocartilage cushion is twisted under load. Soft tissue injuries also include tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis), golfer’s elbow (medial epicondylitis) and abrasions (skin surface injuries from friction).

Key Fact

RICE is the immediate treatment protocol for soft tissue injuries: Rest (stop activity to prevent further damage), Ice (apply for 15–20 minutes to reduce swelling and pain), Compression (bandage to limit swelling), Elevation (raise the injured part above heart level to reduce blood pooling). RICE is applied in the first 24–48 hours after injury.

Key Fact

Seven banned PED categories: anabolic steroids (strength/power), EPO and blood doping (endurance oxygen), growth hormones (muscle mass/fat loss), stimulants (alertness/endurance), narcotic analgesics (pain masking), diuretics (weight loss/masking), beta blockers (precision steadiness). All are banned under WADA rules.

Performance-Enhancing Drugs (PEDs)

Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) are substances used to gain an unfair advantage in sport. They are banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and their use is considered cheating. Each category of PED has specific effects and health risks.

Anabolic steroids are synthetic versions of testosterone. They increase muscle protein synthesis, leading to greater muscle hypertrophy, strength and recovery. They are used in power and strength sports. Health risks include liver damage, cardiovascular disease, hormonal disruption (including reduced fertility), aggression and, in young athletes, early closure of growth plates. Beta blockers reduce heart rate and control tremors. They are used in precision sports such as archery, shooting and snooker. Health risks include lowered blood pressure and bradycardia.

Stimulants increase alertness, concentration and aggression, and delay the onset of fatigue. They include amphetamines and some substances found in cold remedies. Health risks include elevated heart rate, anxiety, cardiac arrhythmia and addiction. Narcotic analgesics are powerful painkillers that allow athletes to compete through injuries that would otherwise force them to stop. They carry risks of addiction, impaired judgement and masking damage that could worsen without rest.

Erythropoietin (EPO) is a peptide hormone that stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells, increasing the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity. This improves aerobic endurance significantly and is used in cycling, marathon running and cross-country skiing. The health risks are severe: increased blood viscosity raises the risk of blood clots, stroke and heart attack. Growth hormones (GH) stimulate muscle growth and fat loss. Health risks include abnormal bone and organ growth (acromegaly) and joint pain. Diuretics increase urine production. They are used either to achieve rapid weight loss for weight-category sports (boxing, judo) or to dilute urine samples in an attempt to hide other banned substances. Health risks include severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. Blood doping involves removing an athlete’s blood, storing it, then re-infusing it before competition to raise red blood cell count. Like EPO, it increases oxygen-carrying capacity and carries similar cardiovascular risks.

PEDs damage sport in two ways: ethically and physically. Ethically, they violate the principles of fair competition — athletes who dope gain an advantage unavailable to those who train within the rules, making meaningful competition impossible. They undermine the values of honesty, integrity and respect that form the foundation of sport. For young athletes, doping also creates a coercive culture: if some competitors dope, those who do not risk being left behind, placing athletes in an unfair dilemma. Physically, every category of PED carries documented health risks. The severity ranges from addiction and cardiovascular disease to potentially fatal blood clotting events associated with EPO and blood doping. Anti-doping testing (urine and blood samples) and biological passport programmes aim to detect PED use and protect the integrity of competition.

A sprain involves a ligament (the tissue connecting bone to bone at a joint). A strain involves a muscle or tendon (the tissue connecting muscle to bone). The confusion arises because both present with pain, swelling and localised bruising. The key question is: where is the damage? A twisted ankle with pain on the outer side of the joint is likely a lateral ligament sprain. A hamstring tear from sprinting is a strain of the muscle belly. Both are treated initially with RICE, but recovery timelines and rehabilitation differ. In the exam, using the wrong term will lose marks — always identify whether the damaged tissue is a ligament or a muscle/tendon.
exam_tip_html: For questions about PEDs, examiners expect you to name the category, state one positive effect on performance and at least one health risk. Writing only “anabolic steroids make you stronger” earns one mark at best; “anabolic steroids increase muscle hypertrophy and strength by raising testosterone levels (1), improving performance in power-based sports; however, they carry health risks including liver damage and cardiovascular disease (1)” earns both. For RICE, be precise: “Ice” means apply cold (15–20 minutes) to reduce swelling and pain by causing vasoconstriction — not just “put ice on it.” For Discuss questions on PEDs that include ethical arguments, always present both sides (performance benefit vs ethical/health cost) to avoid capping at the lower band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A PARQ screens for health conditions before exercise begins; positive answers require medical clearance. Injury prevention also requires correct training principles, protective equipment and facility checks.
  • RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) is the immediate treatment for soft tissue injuries in the first 24–48 hours. Injury types include concussion, fractures, dislocations, sprains (ligament), strains (muscle/tendon) and torn cartilage.
  • PEDs (anabolic steroids, EPO, stimulants, narcotic analgesics, diuretics, beta blockers, growth hormones, blood doping) improve performance in specific ways but carry significant health risks and are banned as unethical in sport.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a sprain?
A) Damage to a muscle or tendon
B) A fracture of the bone at a joint
C) Stretching or tearing of a ligament
D) Displacement of joint bones out of alignment
practice_questions.marks: C) Stretching or tearing of a ligament [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what the letters RICE stand for in the treatment of a soft tissue injury.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any two correct letters with their full term: Rest (1), Ice (1), Compression (1), Elevation (1). Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how EPO (erythropoietin) improves performance in endurance sport and identify one health risk of its use.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: EPO stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells (1); increased red blood cells raise the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, delaying fatigue in endurance events such as cycling or marathon running (1); health risk: increased blood viscosity raises the risk of blood clots, stroke or heart attack (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the purpose of a PARQ and describe one amendment to a training programme that might be recommended if someone answered 'yes' to a question about recent chest pain.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: a PARQ screens individuals for medical conditions that could make vigorous exercise unsafe before they begin training (1); its purpose is to identify anyone who needs medical clearance before starting a programme (1); an amendment for chest pain might be to advise the person to consult a doctor and, pending clearance, restrict initial training to very low-intensity activity (e.g. gentle walking) to avoid placing excessive demand on the cardiovascular system (1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level weightlifter is considering using anabolic steroids to improve her performance before a national competition. Discuss the positive effects on performance and the negative consequences of using anabolic steroids in this context.
practice_questions.marks: Positive (up to 2 marks): anabolic steroids increase muscle protein synthesis, leading to greater muscle hypertrophy and strength (1); they also speed up recovery between training sessions, allowing greater training frequency and volume before competition (1). Negative (up to 2 marks): health risks include liver damage, cardiovascular disease and hormonal disruption including infertility (1); use is banned under WADA rules and would result in disqualification, loss of results and potential lifetime ban (1).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which injury prevention strategies can protect a 16-year-old recreational football player from injury throughout a full season.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For â€” correct application of training principles (progressive overload, rest days) prevents overuse injuries like shin splints and tendinopathy; using protective equipment (shin pads, appropriate boots) reduces traumatic soft tissue injuries during contact; completing a PARQ ensures any pre-existing conditions are managed; following the rules of football minimises dangerous tackles. Against â€” not all injuries are preventable: unpredictable contact injuries (sprains from awkward landings, concussions from clashes) occur even with all protocols in place; the environment (pitch quality, weather) contributes to injury risk; adolescent bone growth makes stress injuries more likely regardless of programme design. Conclusion: prevention strategies substantially reduce injury risk and frequency, but cannot eliminate it entirely; the most effective approach combines physical preparation, safe environment, correct equipment and adherence to the rules. Balanced, applied to football throughout, concluded.

Secure: Addresses both preventable and unpreventable aspects. Football application present. Reaches conclusion.

Developing: Lists strategies without full evaluation. Some sporting application.

Emerging: Names one strategy or injury. Minimal evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the 'E' in RICE stand for?
Which category of PED works by stimulating red blood cell production to increase oxygen-carrying capacity?
A _____ is a stretching or tearing of a ligament at a joint, most commonly the ankle.
The PARQ (Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire) is completed before starting a new programme to identify any _____ reasons that might require medical clearance.
Match each PED category to its primary use or effect in sport:
right: Increase muscle mass, strength and recovery rate
Reduce heart rate and control tremors in precision sports

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of a PARQ?
flashcard_questions.a: To screen individuals for medical conditions before they begin a new exercise programme.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a sprain and a strain?
flashcard_questions.a: Sprain = ligament damage; strain = muscle or tendon damage.
When joint bones are forced out of their normal alignment, tearing the joint capsule.

flashcard_questions.q: How do anabolic steroids improve performance?
flashcard_questions.a: By increasing muscle protein synthesis, leading to greater strength and faster recovery.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one health risk of anabolic steroid use?
flashcard_questions.a: Liver damage, cardiovascular disease or hormonal disruption (accept any one).

flashcard_questions.q: How does EPO improve endurance performance?
flashcard_questions.a: It stimulates red blood cell production, increasing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.

flashcard_questions.q: Which precision sports are beta blockers used in, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Archery and shooting, because they reduce heart rate and control hand tremors.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are diuretics banned in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: They can mask other banned substances by diluting urine, and cause rapid weight loss.
Removing, storing and re-infusing an athlete's blood to raise red blood cell count before competition.

flashcard_questions.q: What is concussion, and what is the immediate action protocol?
flashcard_questions.a: A brain injury from a blow to the head; the athlete must be removed from play immediately.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two injury prevention strategies beyond warm-up and cool-down.
flashcard_questions.a: Using protective equipment and checking facilities/equipment before use.

glossary_terms.definition: A Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire: a short health-screening tool used to identify any medical reasons why someone might need medical clearance before beginning exercise.
A traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head that disrupts normal brain function; symptoms include headache, confusion, dizziness and nausea.
A break in a bone, ranging from a stress fracture (hairline crack) to a complete break.
A joint injury in which the bones are forced out of their normal alignment, tearing the surrounding joint capsule and ligaments.
A stretching or tearing of the ligaments that support a joint, most commonly the ankle or knee.
A stretching or tearing of a muscle or tendon, also called a muscle pull.
Substances taken to gain an unfair advantage in sport by improving performance, strength, endurance or recovery beyond natural training adaptations.
Synthetic versions of testosterone used to increase muscle mass, strength and recovery rate; carry health risks including liver damage, cardiovascular disease and hormonal disruption.
Medications that block the effects of adrenaline, reducing heart rate and anxiety; used in precision sports but prohibited in events where steadiness is an advantage.
Drugs that increase alertness, reaction time and aggression; used to delay fatigue during endurance events.
Painkillers derived from opium that mask pain signals, allowing athletes to compete through injury.
A peptide hormone produced naturally by the kidneys that stimulates red blood cell production; synthetic EPO is used to increase oxygen-carrying capacity in endurance events.
Synthetic versions of human growth hormone used to increase muscle mass and reduce body fat; associated with abnormal tissue growth and joint pain.
Drugs that increase urine production, used to mask the presence of other banned substances or to achieve rapid weight loss for weight-class sports.
The practice of removing and storing an athlete's own blood before competition, then re-infusing it to increase red blood cell count and oxygen-carrying capacity.
